It is important to be clear that this comparison is deliberately narrow in its scope: it does not extend to any other property of the materials, and any conclusion drawn from it is correspondingly limited. Within that scope, the material that possesses the higher temperature limit is the preferred material, since the joint must be capable of withstanding the temperatures that arise in service with an adequate margin held in reserve.

The gasket comparison for the absorber joints covers two materials on temperature limit only. The comparison is narrow by design: no other property is assessed, and the preference it produces extends no further than the criterion applied. On temperature limit, the higher-rated material is preferred. The rated limit is the ceiling the joint must stay below in service, and the higher rating holds the larger margin against the service temperature. Joints do not fail at the rating in ordinary operation; they fail where the margin has been consumed, and a selection made on temperature limit is a selection of margin before it is a selection of material.

The absorber wall thickness is 42 mm after the corrosion allowance is added, and that figure is the thickness carried into fabrication. The allowance is not spare metal added for comfort: it is the loss the wall is expected to sustain over the service life, included so that the thickness at the end of life still meets the design requirement. The compressor and the lean solvent pump follow the same allowance rule in their own subsections. The rule is uniform because the duty is uniform in kind: every wall in the section loses material to the same service, and a section that allowed one rule for one vessel and another rule for the next would produce thicknesses that could not be compared across the section it specifies.

The gasket preference, stated on one criterion, leaves the governing question open. A joint is selected against everything it must withstand, and temperature is one item in that list.
